triage.name: Back Pain
triage.reason: Extremely common symptom presentation; workup centers on red flags and distinguishing mechanical pain from radiculopathy, malignancy or infection, making it a strong undifferentiated case.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: One of the most common reasons for primary care and emergency department visits in the US
Slightly more common and more disabling in women in some surveys
More prevalent among adults with physically demanding jobs or low job control

risk_factors.text: Heavy or repetitive lifting, bending or twisting at work
Prolonged sitting or whole-body vibration (long-distance driving)

family_history: Back pain in a parent or sibling
social_history: Low job satisfaction or high job strain
Limited access to care or physically inactive lifestyle

chief_complaints.text: It hurts to bend over or lift things
The pain shoots down my leg

hpi.onset: Usually gradual after activity, lifting or a change in routine; sometimes sudden after a specific movement or minor injury
hpi.duration: Acute episodes typically a few days to a few weeks; chronic if more than three months
hpi.progression: Often improves over days to weeks with activity as tolerated; may wax and wane or become persistent
hpi.location: Lower back (lumbosacral region) most often; can be mid-back or upper back
hpi.radiation: Usually none; when present, radiates into the buttock, posterior thigh and below the knee in a dermatomal pattern
hpi.quality: Dull, aching or stiff; sharp with certain movements
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate, typically 3–7/10; severe with acute muscle spasm
hpi.timing: Worse with movement, lifting, bending, prolonged sitting or standing; better with rest or position change

associated_symptoms.text: Stiffness, especially in the morning or after inactivity
Numbness or tingling in the leg or foot
Weakness in the leg or foot

pertinent_negatives: Loss of bowel or bladder control
Night pain that wakes from sleep
Age over 50 with new onset pain

positives.text: Limited range of motion due to pain

negatives: Point tenderness over the spine suggesting fracture

positives.text: Numbness or tingling in a leg or foot

atypical.how_it_differs: Back pain in children is uncommon and more often has an identifiable cause such as spondylolysis, infection or tumor; children may present with refusal to walk or irritability rather than a clear pain description.
missing_classic_features: Typical adult pattern of activity-related pain

atypical.how_it_differs: More likely to have degenerative changes, spinal stenosis or compression fracture; pain may be less activity-related and more constant, and serious causes are more common.
Pain is often in the lumbosacral region or posterior pelvis, worse with prolonged standing or walking, and may be accompanied by pelvic girdle pain; red flags still require the same evaluation.
Higher mechanical load and deconditioning can make pain more persistent and less responsive to activity; weight loss is often part of management.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, moves slowly but without distress
general.moderate: Guarded posture, shifts weight or stands with a flattened lumbar curve, grimaces when rising from a chair
general.severe: Visibly uncomfortable, splints the back, needs help getting on and off the exam table
general.critical: Distressed or toxic-appearing, may be unable to bear weight or sit up; consider infection, fracture or cauda equina

findings.maneuver: Palpate the paraspinal muscles on both sides of the lumbar spine
findings.finding: Tenderness and tightness of the paraspinal musculature without focal bony tenderness

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to bend forward, then extend, side-bend and rotate the trunk
findings.finding: Pain-limited range of motion, worst with forward flexion

findings.maneuver: Palpate the lumbar paraspinal muscles while the patient stands
findings.finding: Firm, board-like paraspinal spasm with loss of the normal lumbar lordosis

findings.maneuver: Palpate and percuss each spinous process from the thoracic spine to the sacrum
findings.finding: No focal point tenderness over a spinous process

findings.maneuver: With the patient supine, raise each extended leg by the heel until pain or tightness occurs
findings.finding: No reproduction of radiating leg pain below about 60 degrees

findings.maneuver: With the patient supine, raise the symptomatic extended leg by the heel
findings.finding: Reproduction of radiating pain down the posterior thigh and below the knee at 30–70 degrees

findings.maneuver: Raise the asymptomatic leg while the patient is supine
findings.finding: Reproduction of pain in the symptomatic leg

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick in the L2–S1 dermatomes of both legs
findings.finding: Decreased sensation in a single dermatome consistent with a nerve root

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick in the L2–S1 dermatomes of both legs
findings.finding: Sensation intact and symmetric in both legs

findings.maneuver: Test ankle dorsiflexion strength against resistance (L4–L5)
findings.finding: Weakness of foot dorsiflexion

findings.maneuver: Test ankle plantarflexion strength against resistance (S1)
findings.finding: Weakness of ankle plantarflexion

findings.maneuver: Test hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion against resistance
findings.finding: Motor strength 5/5 and symmetric in both legs

findings.maneuver: Check the patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes
findings.finding: Reflexes 2+ and symmetric

findings.maneuver: Check the Achilles deep tendon reflex
findings.finding: Diminished or absent Achilles reflex on the affected side (S1)

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient walking, then ask them to walk on the heels and on the toes
findings.finding: Steady, symmetric gait without foot drop

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient walking
findings.finding: Antalgic or guarded gait favoring the painful side

findings.maneuver: Test light touch over the perineum, inner thighs and buttocks (saddle distribution)
findings.finding: Sensation intact in the saddle distribution

findings.maneuver: Test light touch over the perineum, inner thighs and buttocks (saddle distribution)
findings.finding: Reduced or absent sensation in the saddle distribution

findings.maneuver: Digital rectal exam assessing resting sphincter tone and voluntary squeeze
findings.finding: Normal resting tone and voluntary contraction

findings.maneuver: Digital rectal exam assessing resting sphincter tone and voluntary squeeze
findings.finding: Decreased resting tone or inability to voluntarily contract the sphincter

findings.maneuver: Percuss the costovertebral angles bilaterally
findings.finding: No costovertebral angle tenderness

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen and feel for a pulsatile epigastric mass in older patients
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without a pulsatile mass

findings.maneuver: Observe general appearance and check temperature
findings.finding: No fever, chills or toxic appearance

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the spine for vesicles, dimpling or a tuft of hair
findings.finding: Intact skin without rash, dimple or hair tuft over the spine

labs.caveat: Nonspecific; a markedly elevated ESR or CRP in an older adult with new back pain raises concern for infection or malignancy.
Usually normal in uncomplicated mechanical back pain; elevation should prompt evaluation for infection or malignancy.
Leukocytosis is not expected in mechanical back pain and suggests spinal infection.
Elevated in Paget disease of bone and in bony metastases.
Hypercalcemia suggests malignancy with bone involvement.
Hematuria points toward a renal or urinary source rather than a spinal one.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
No acute ischemic changes; ECG is normal in uncomplicated mechanical back pain

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected fracture, older adults with new pain, or trauma

findings.text: Normal vertebral alignment and disc heights
Degenerative disc space narrowing and osteophyte formation
Vertebral compression fracture with loss of anterior height
Vertebral body destruction or lytic lesion suggesting malignancy

imaging.preferred_when: Red flags, progressive neurologic deficit, or failure of conservative care

findings.text: Disc bulge or herniation with nerve root compression
Degenerative disc disease and facet arthropathy
Discitis or vertebral osteomyelitis with marrow edema and enhancement
Vertebral body marrow replacement suggesting metastasis
Cauda equina compression with crowded nerve roots

imaging.preferred_when: When MRI is contraindicated or unavailable

findings.text: Degenerative changes, facet hypertrophy and disc space narrowing

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected occult fracture, infection or metastasis when MRI is not possible

findings.text: Focal increased radiotracer uptake in a vertebral body

imaging.preferred_when: Flank or abdominal pain suggesting a renal or aortic source

initial.why: The core of evaluation: identify red flags, neurologic deficits and mechanical versus radicular pattern
Rules out pregnancy before any imaging
Screens for fracture or bony lesion
initial.only_if: red flags such as trauma, older age, osteoporosis or corticosteroid use
red flags such as fever, weight loss, night pain or age over 50 with new pain

initial.why: Adds to ESR when infection or malignancy is suspected
Looks for leukocytosis or anemia suggesting infection or malignancy
Evaluates for urinary infection or stone when pain is flank-predominant

confirmatory.why: Best test for nerve root compression, stenosis, infection, malignancy and cauda equina
confirmatory.only_if: red flags, progressive neurologic deficit, or persistent symptoms despite conservative care

supporting.why: Alternative when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable
Detects occult fracture, infection or metastasis
supporting.only_if: MRI is not possible and a bony source is suspected

supporting.why: Evaluates for renal or aortic cause of back/flank pain
supporting.only_if: flank or abdominal pain suggests a renal or vascular source

not_indicated.why: No role in back pain evaluation
Not needed unless pain is epigastric or suggests pancreatitis
Not indicated unless chest pain or cardiac symptoms are present

decision_points: Screen for red flags (cauda equina, fracture, infection, malignancy) before ordering imaging
Pregnancy test before any imaging in anyone who could be pregnant
Cauda equina syndrome or progressive neurologic deficit requires emergent MRI and surgical consultation
Do not order routine imaging in acute mechanical back pain without red flags

differential.name: Cauda equina syndrome
differential.why_considered: Severe low back pain with bilateral leg symptoms, saddle numbness, or bladder/bowel dysfunction
differential.trigger: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, or bilateral leg weakness with back pain

exam: Absent or reduced deep tendon reflexes in the legs
labs: No specific lab finding; diagnosis is clinical and imaging-based
imaging: MRI showing compression of the cauda equina with crowded nerve roots
Large central disc herniation, epidural mass, or spinal stenosis at multiple levels

differential.name: Vertebral compression fracture
differential.why_considered: Acute, focal back pain in an older adult or after minor trauma
differential.trigger: Age over 50, osteoporosis, chronic corticosteroid use, or minor trauma with focal spinal tenderness

history: Sudden onset after a fall, lifting, or even coughing
Pain worse with sitting up or standing, better lying flat
History of osteoporosis or long-term corticosteroid use
exam: Focal tenderness over a spinous process
Loss of height or new kyphosis
Pain reproduced by gentle percussion over the affected vertebra
labs: Normal unless there is an underlying malignancy or infection
imaging: X-ray showing loss of vertebral body height with cortical buckling
MRI showing bone marrow edema in the fractured vertebra

differential.name: Spinal epidural abscess
differential.why_considered: Back pain with fever, night pain, or progressive neurologic deficits
differential.trigger: Fever, intravenous drug use, recent spinal procedure, or progressive neurologic deficit

history: Intravenous drug use, recent bacteremia, or spinal surgery/injection
Severe, unrelenting pain that wakes from sleep
Progressive weakness or numbness over hours to days
exam: Neurologic deficits corresponding to the level of compression
imaging: MRI with contrast showing an epidural fluid collection with rim enhancement

differential.name: Vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis
differential.why_considered: Insidious back pain with fever, night pain, or risk factors for infection
differential.trigger: Fever, intravenous drug use, recent bacteremia, or immunosuppression with new back pain

history: Risk factors: diabetes, immunosuppression, intravenous drug use, recent infection
exam: Pain with any movement of the spine
imaging: MRI showing disc space narrowing, marrow edema, and enhancement of the disc and adjacent vertebral bodies

differential.name: Malignancy (metastatic disease or multiple myeloma)
differential.why_considered: Back pain in a patient with a history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, or night pain
differential.trigger: History of cancer, unexplained weight loss, night pain, or age over 50 with new back pain

history: Known primary cancer (breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid)
Unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or night sweats
Pain that is constant and worse at night, not relieved by rest
imaging: X-ray showing lytic or sclerotic lesions
MRI showing marrow replacement and possible epidural extension
Bone scan showing multiple areas of increased uptake

differential.name: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
differential.why_considered: Mid-back or flank pain in an older adult, especially with cardiovascular risk factors
differential.trigger: Age over 60, smoking history, pulsatile abdominal mass, or sudden severe back pain

history: Sudden onset of severe, tearing mid-back or abdominal pain
History of hypertension, smoking, or known aneurysm
labs: No specific lab finding; may have anemia if ruptured
imaging: CT angiography showing aneurysm size and possible rupture

differential.name: Kidney stone or pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Flank pain radiating to the groin, often with urinary symptoms

history: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
labs: Pyuria and positive urine culture if infection
imaging: CT or ultrasound showing renal stone and hydronephrosis

differential.name: Pancreatitis
differential.why_considered: Mid-back pain radiating from the epigastrium, often with nausea and vomiting

history: Epigastric pain radiating to the back
imaging: CT showing pancreatic inflammation or fluid collections

differential.name: Herpes zoster (shingles)
differential.why_considered: Unilateral burning or shooting back pain preceding a rash

exam: Vesicular rash in a dermatomal pattern
labs: Clinical diagnosis; PCR of vesicle fluid if needed

differential.name: Ankylosing spondylitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic back pain in a young adult, worse at rest and better with exercise

history: Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
imaging: X-ray showing sacroiliitis and bamboo spine

severity.mild: Acute, self-limited mechanical pain: discomfort with movement, no radiation, no neurologic deficits, able to perform daily activities with minor limitation
severity.moderate: More persistent pain with muscle spasm, limited range of motion, some difficulty with work or sleep, but no red flags or neurologic deficits
severity.severe: Severe pain with muscle spasm, significant functional limitation, possible radicular symptoms, but no cauda equina or progressive neurologic deficit
severity.critical: Back pain with red flags: cauda equina syndrome, spinal infection, fracture with neurologic compromise, or malignancy with cord compression; requires emergent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence
red_flags.meaning: Cauda equina syndrome; emergent MRI and surgical consultation
Significant nerve root or cord compression; urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Fever, chills, or night sweats with back pain
red_flags.meaning: Spinal infection (epidural abscess, osteomyelitis, discitis); urgent MRI and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Unexplained weight loss, night pain, or history of cancer
red_flags.meaning: Malignancy with possible spinal metastasis; urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: Age over 50 with new back pain, or minor trauma with focal spinal tenderness
Intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, or recent bacteremia
Sudden severe tearing mid-back pain with pulsatile abdominal mass
red_flags.meaning: Abdominal aortic aneurysm; emergent vascular evaluation

special_populations.differences: Back pain in children is uncommon and more often has an identifiable cause such as spondylolysis, infection, or tumor; children may present with refusal to walk or irritability rather than a clear pain description.
More likely to have degenerative changes, spinal stenosis, or compression fracture; pain may be less activity-related and more constant, and serious causes are more common.
Pain is often in the lumbosacral region or posterior pelvis, worse with prolonged standing or walking, and may be accompanied by pelvic girdle pain; red flags still require the same evaluation.
Higher mechanical load and deconditioning can make pain more persistent and less responsive to activity; weight loss is often part of management.

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and does it stay in your back or travel anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Lumbosacral location; radiation into the buttock, posterior thigh, or below the knee suggests radiculopathy

key_questions.question: When did it start, and was there a specific movement, lift, or injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual or sudden onset after activity or minor trauma; no trauma suggests mechanical or other cause

key_questions.question: How long has it been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute (days to weeks) versus chronic (more than three months)

key_questions.question: What makes it better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with bending, lifting, prolonged sitting or standing; better with rest or position change

key_questions.question: Does the pain wake you from sleep or occur at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Night pain that wakes from sleep suggests infection or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you had any loss of bladder or bowel control, or trouble urinating?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary retention or incontinence suggests cauda equina syndrome

key_questions.question: Any numbness or tingling in the groin, inner thighs, or buttocks?
key_questions.looking_for: Saddle anesthesia suggests cauda equina syndrome

key_questions.question: Any weakness in your legs, or has your foot been dragging?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive or severe leg weakness suggests nerve root or cord compression

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or chills suggest spinal infection

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss suggests malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: History of cancer raises concern for spinal metastasis

key_questions.question: Have you ever used intravenous drugs, or had a recent infection or spinal procedure?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for spinal infection

key_questions.question: Do you take corticosteroids regularly, or have you been told you have osteoporosis?
key_questions.looking_for: Increased risk of vertebral compression fracture

key_questions.question: Have you had a fall or other injury to your back?
key_questions.looking_for: Trauma raises concern for fracture

key_questions.question: What do you do for work, and does it involve heavy lifting or prolonged sitting?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational strain and job control influence risk and recovery

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, and how much alcohol do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking and alcohol use affect bone health and recovery

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have back problems or arthritis of the spine?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of back pain or ankylosing spondylitis

key_questions.question: Any burning or shooting pain in a band around your chest or back, or a rash?
key_questions.looking_for: Dermatomal pain preceding a rash suggests herpes zoster

key_questions.question: Any trouble with urination, blood in the urine, or flank pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary symptoms suggest a renal source

key_questions.question: Any abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Abdominal symptoms suggest pancreatitis or another abdominal source

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy must be excluded before imaging

reasoning_points: Pain is in the lumbosacral region, worse with movement and better with rest, consistent with a mechanical pattern
No red flags: no saddle anesthesia, no bowel or bladder dysfunction, no fever, no weight loss, no cancer history, no significant trauma
No progressive or severe leg weakness and no foot drop
Neurologic exam is intact: normal strength, sensation, reflexes, and gait
No focal spinal tenderness or point tenderness over a spinous process
No costovertebral angle tenderness and no abdominal tenderness or pulsatile mass
Imaging is not indicated in uncomplicated mechanical back pain without red flags

easy: Young or middle-aged adult with acute onset after lifting
Pain limited to the lower back without radiation
No red flags and a normal neurologic exam
medium: Radicular pain radiating below the knee with a positive straight leg raise
Older adult with new back pain but no red flags
Pregnancy with lumbosacral and pelvic girdle pain
Patient with obesity and persistent pain despite conservative care
hard: Older adult with a compression fracture after minor trauma or corticosteroid use
Fever, night pain, and leukocytosis suggesting spinal infection
History of cancer with night pain and weight loss suggesting metastasis
Saddle anesthesia or urinary retention suggesting cauda equina syndrome
Sudden severe tearing mid-back pain with a pulsatile abdominal mass suggesting aortic aneurysm
